column3: The exact reply moves disputation to Allah's fuller knowledge of what the opponents do.
Noah likewise refuses to claim knowledge of people's deeds, reserving that judgment beyond the messenger.
Shuayb directly says his Lord encompasses what his people do, closely restating the focus's accountability claim.
Moses' address to Pharaoh locates prophetic authority in the Lord of all worlds rather than the ruler.
Moses leaves recognition of guidance and final outcome to his Lord's superior knowledge.
The universal Lordship title supplies only the broad authority underlying the focus.

Pharaoh's question about the two messengers' Lord supplies only a general authority setting.
Allah's fuller knowledge of the opponents' descriptions tempers their accusation, though not their deeds specifically.
The invalidated works motif does not clarify the messenger's deference to divine knowledge.
Moses' trust that his Lord will guide gives a nearby prophetic reliance on the same divine authority.

Naming Moses and Aaron's Lord adds no new knowledge-of-deeds element.
God's knowledge of opponents' descriptions supports answering evil with what is better.

The described reward does not clarify the focus's knowledge or reply.
Pharaoh's question about the Lord of all worlds supplies the local authority confrontation behind Shuayb's appeal to his Lord.
God's knowledgeable witness to revelation supports a prophet's answer to accusations.
Divine knowledge of what people say is related but less specific than knowledge of their deeds.
Exalting the Lord's name does not add an identifiable element of the focus.
Because God knows what opponents say, the messenger need not compel them and should only remind.
Each soul's knowledge of what it brought supplies an accountability counterpart to the focus.
Reward for past deeds is only a general consequence after stronger accountability cards.
Actions expose tested loyalty under God's informed knowledge, rather than give God new information.

Disclosure and punishment for deeds give only a general outcome of wrongdoing.
God's knowledge beyond human knowledge provides a broad model for the focus's deferential claim.
Cosmic Lordship adds no specific knowledge or accountability element.
Condemnation for denying signs without encompassing their knowledge links deficient knowing to what people do.

The warning that people will know adds no distinct action-accountability detail.
Allah's knowledge of what was delivered is too context-specific to add to the focus.
The Lord's cosmic dominion is too general after earlier authority cards.
Allah's knowledge of concealed disbelief supports the focus's judgment beyond public claims.
The future-knowledge warning is redundant and nonspecific about deeds.
God knows how opponents listen and what they privately say about the messenger.
God's all-encompassing knowledge and sight of deeds supplies a broad but direct frame.
Knowledge of actions closes a legal instruction but does not illuminate the focus reply.
The repeated warning adds no new connection beyond the preceding card.

The workers' reward is a generic result of deeds.
Return to the Knower of unseen and seen brings a report of what people did.
Messengers are commanded to do righteous deeds under the declaration that God knows what they do.

Divine hearing and knowledge support seeking refuge in conflict, but not the focus's assessment of deeds.
Excuses yield to deeds seen by God and reported on return to the Knower of unseen and seen.

God's knowledge of deeds underwrites truthful testimony and entrusted conduct.
The repeated naming of Moses and Aaron's Lord adds no new element.
God's exclusive knowledge of the unseen is joined to exclusive judgment, supporting the focus's deference.
Recompense for evil and good deeds supplies the general outcome of the actions in the focus.

Preservation of reward for good works is a generic consequence rather than a knowledge claim.
God knows the concealed action of those who treat Joseph as merchandise.
An appeal for increased punishment does not clarify divine knowledge of the community's deeds.
The confession of the Lord of all worlds repeats a generic authority point already covered.
Return to the Lord gives an eschatological frame without specifying deeds or knowledge.

Destruction for earnings only loosely supplies a consequence of action.
Life and death test which deeds are best, providing a broad basis for evaluating actions.
A speaker recalling a companion does not clarify the focus.
Transcending people's descriptions loosely parallels God knowing more than their claims.
The exchange of greetings does not add to the focus.
A book detailed with knowledge supports revealed guidance generally, not the focus's judgment of deeds.
Shuayb's command to give full measure identifies the concrete deeds whose accountability frames the focus reply.
The command to weigh with a sound balance continues the immediate ethical standard for the people's actions.
The prohibition on defrauding people and spreading corruption names the wrongdoing behind "what you do."
Calling them to fear their Creator grounds Shuayb's appeal to his Lord in created dependence.
The charge that Shuayb is bewitched begins the hostile speech to which his deferred answer responds.
Calling him a liar and demanding proof makes clear why he refuses to make himself the final judge.
Their demand for a fragment of heaven to fall is the immediate provocation answered by 26:188.
Their denial and the punishment of the overshadowing day state the outcome of the rejected warning.
The parallel Madyan account identifies Shuayb's people and joins worship of God to their commercial conduct.
Shuayb's command for full measure and balance closely specifies the conduct at issue in the focus scene.
He forbids corruption after reform, giving the moral content of the people's deeds.
The people's mocking question about Shuayb's prayer and ancestral practice develops the resistance behind his reply.
Shuayb disclaims private interest and states that he seeks reform only as far as he can.
He warns that opposition to him must not bring on them the fate of earlier peoples.
The call to seek forgiveness and repent supplies the corrective response to their conduct.
Their claim not to understand him and threat of stoning show the audience's escalating rejection.
Shuayb tells his people to act from their position and await knowledge of who will receive disgrace.
Shuayb's rescue and the seizure of the wrongdoers give the narrative resolution of the warning.
The destruction of Madyan completes the judgment on the people whose deeds God encompassed.
Allah knows what people conceal and reveal, directly supporting knowledge beyond their public claims.
What is within selves is known to God and subject to His judgment, widening the focus beyond outward acts.
Whether people conceal or reveal, Allah knows it; this supports Shuayb's refusal to rely on appearances.
Allah's knowledge of what is in breasts exposes the difference between spoken claims and hidden thought.
The messenger's duty is delivery while Allah knows what people reveal and conceal, closely defining the messenger's limit.
Jesus leaves knowledge of the unseen to God, a prophetic model of epistemic restraint.
Allah knows secret and public matters and knows what people earn, directly joining knowledge with deeds.
Return to God brings disclosure of what people were doing, supplying the final accountability horizon.
The Lord knows best who strays and who is guided, a close parallel to the focus's deferred assessment.
Each has degrees for what they did, and the Lord is not heedless of their deeds.
The command to act from one's position and await the outcome parallels Shuayb's answer to defiant opponents.
Those who received messengers and the messengers themselves will be questioned, extending accountability to the prophetic encounter.
God will recount events to them with knowledge, directly linking judgment to complete divine awareness.
No deed, recitation, or action escapes the Lord's witnessing, a comprehensive direct parallel.
The Lord knows hidden matters and is not heedless of what people do, uniting unseen knowledge with action.
Allah knows what people do in their covenants, placing conduct under explicit divine knowledge.
God will make known to people what they were doing, supplying the judgment implicit in the focus.
God knows the secret and what is still more hidden, strengthening the scope of the focus's claim.
Each soul is recompensed for what it strives for, giving the end toward which accountable deeds lead.
The prophet answers opponents by saying his Lord knows every word in heaven and earth.
God knows spoken words and what people conceal, directly qualifying a disputed prophetic address.
God knows the condition people are in and will report to them what they did when they return to Him.
The prophet answers the fabrication charge by appealing to the One who knows the secret of heaven and earth.
The Lord knows what breasts conceal and what people disclose, extending the focus beyond visible conduct.
The Lord is not heedless of what people do, directly echoing the focus's action-accountability premise.
Against disbelief in revelation, the prophet invokes God's sufficient witness and comprehensive knowledge.
The Knower of the unseen misses nothing, providing a broad basis for the focus's certainty.
God knows the unseen of heaven and earth and the contents of breasts, supporting full moral assessment.
God records what people send ahead and their traces, making deeds enduring evidence.
The Knower of unseen and seen is asked to judge disputed servants, paralleling the focus's refusal of self-judgment.
God knows the furtive glance and what breasts conceal, giving a concentrated statement of hidden accountability.
God accepts repentance and knows what people do, joining moral return to complete awareness of conduct.
God hears private counsel and secret speech, exposing the opponents' mistaken confidence in concealment.
God knows every private conference and is with people wherever they are, then informs them of their deeds.
Each soul must consider what it has sent ahead, for God is fully aware of what people do.
God knows what is in heaven and earth, secret and public, and what lies within breasts.
Whether speech is hidden or public, God knows the contents of breasts.
God encompasses all things in knowledge, supplying the widest basis for the focus's appeal to his Lord.
